Adrian Roselli - ARIA Live Regions & Status Messages

title: Color as Only Visual Indicator
desc: Information is communicated using color alone. For example, a required field is highlighted in red but has no other indicator. People who are colorblind or cannot see colors will miss this information.
fix: Add a non-color indicator alongside the color cue ,  for example, an icon, pattern, text label, border, or underline. Required fields should include an asterisk or the word "required" in the label. Error states should include an inline error message or icon, not just a red border. Links in body text should be underlined or otherwise visually distinct from surrounding text without relying on color alone. Charts and graphs should use patterns or labels in addition to color to distinguish data series.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.1: Use of Color (Level A)
Alistair Campbell - Color Vision Research

fix: Remove `user-scalable="no"` from the viewport meta tag. Set `maximum-scale` to at least `2`. Allow full browser zoom.
title: Zooming and Scaling Disabled
desc: Zooming is disabled or restricted (`user-scalable="no"` or `maximum-scale` less than 2x). Low-vision users cannot magnify content.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.4: Resize Text (Level AA)
Deque University - meta-viewport

fix: Use `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, or the `hidden` attribute to hide content from users and AT. Use `aria-hidden="true"` only for decorative content that remains visually visible. Never use it on interactive elements. Ensure collapsible sections properly remove hidden content from the accessibility tree.
title: Improperly Hidden Content
desc: Content meant to be hidden remains accessible to assistive technology or keyboard users. CSS hide techniques are incomplete.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Info and Relationships (Level A)
Deque University - Hidden content on the page should be analyzed

title: Text Spacing Too Tight
desc: The page does not support minimum text spacing. When users apply custom spacing through browser settings, content breaks or becomes unreadable.
fix: Design and code so the page still works with these values applied: line height at least 1.5� the font size, paragraph spacing at least 2� the font size, letter spacing at least 0.12� the font size, word spacing at least 0.16� the font size.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.12: Text Spacing (Level AA)
Adrian Roselli - Variable Fonts and Dyslexia

title: Language Change Not Marked in HTML
desc: The page contains text in more than one language, but the language change is not marked in the HTML. Screen readers read foreign words using the wrong pronunciation.
fix: Add a lang attribute to the element wrapping the text in a different language. For example: Hola.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.1.2: Language of Parts (Level AA)

title: Page Language Not Set
desc: The html element has no lang attribute. Screen readers use the wrong language profile to read the page, causing incorrect pronunciation.
fix: Add a lang attribute to the html element that matches the primary language of the page. For example: <html lang="en">.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.1.1: Language of Page (Level A)

fix: Provide a single-pointer or keyboard-accessible alternative to any drag interaction. Examples: sliders accept typed values or +/- buttons; reorderable lists use up/down arrow buttons; map panning use directional buttons. Test that the alternative achieves the same functionality.
title: Dragging Movements Not Keyboard Accessible
desc: Dragging a pointer is required, but users with motor impairments or alternative input methods cannot perform it. Even keyboard controls not provide equivalent functionality.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.7: Dragging Movements (Level AA)
2.5.7 Dragging Movements | Level AA
WebAIM: Keyboard Accessibility

title: Endless Animation Loop
desc: An animation or moving element starts automatically and loops without stopping. There is no way for the user to pause, stop, or hide it. This be distracting or harmful for people with certain conditions.
fix: Provide a visible, keyboard-accessible button to pause or stop the animation. Or set it to stop automatically within 5 seconds. If the animation conveys live data (like a news ticker), a pause button is required.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A)
Scott Vinkle - Providing an Accessible User Experience with Animation

title: Keyboard Trap
desc: Keyboard focus gets stuck inside a component. Once a keyboard-only user tabs into it, there is no way out using only the keyboard.
fix: Make sure keyboard-only users always tab out of any component. If a modal or dialog traps focus intentionally, add an Escape key handler and a visible close button so users leave.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.2: No Keyboard Trap (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - Dialog Focus in Screen Readers

fix: Provide text alternatives: brief alt text (chart type, key finding), longer description (data, trends, insights), and data table. Ensure 4.5:1 contrast on text; don't rely on color alone. Make interactive elements keyboard accessible with clear focus indicators.
title: Inaccessible Data Visualization
desc: Charts and graphs are inaccessible outside of their visible, graphical format. The data and insights they convey are not available to users of assistive technology.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: Non-text Content (Level A)
How to make interactive charts accessible

title: Tabular Data Without Table Markup
desc: Data organized in rows and columns is not using HTML table markup. Screen reader users cannot understand the relationship between column headers and data cells.
fix: Use proper table markup with table, thead, tbody, tr, th, and td elements. Make sure column and row headers use th elements with appropriate scope attributes.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Info and Relationships (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - Data Tables

title: Hover Content Not Keyboard Accessible
scLabel: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
desc: Extra content appears only when the user hovers with a mouse. keyboard-only users and screen reader users cannot trigger or read this content.
fix: Make hover content also appear when the element receives keyboard focus. Users must be able to dismiss it without moving focus (for example, with Escape). The content should stay visible until the user moves focus away.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.13: Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
Adrian Roselli - More on Hover vs. Touch

fix: Add visible `<label for="id">` paired with `<input id="id">`. If visible label is not possible, use aria-label (not placeholder). Test that clicking the label focuses the input.
title: Unlabeled Form Inputs
desc: Form fields and other controls are missing discrete visible labels. The placeholder field alone is not sufficient as a programmatically associated label.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.2: Labels or Instructions (Level A)
WebAIM: Creating Accessible Forms - Accessible Form Controls
WebAIM: Decoding Label and Name for Accessibility

title: No Warning Before Link Opens New Window
desc: A link or button opens a new browser window or tab without warning. This is disorienting, especially for screen reader users who not realize the context has changed.
fix: Add a warning in the link text or accessible name. For example: "Annual Report (opens in a new tab)". You also add an icon with alt text to indicate a new window will open.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.2.2: On Input (Level A)

title: Receiving Focus Causes Unexpected Change
desc: When an element receives keyboard or pointer focus, the page changes ,  for example, a form submits or a new page loads. This is unexpected and disorienting.
fix: Do not trigger any actions when an element receives focus. Actions should only happen when the user deliberately activates a control (for example, by pressing Enter, Space, or clicking).

links.text: Understanding SC 3.2.1: On Focus (Level A)

title: Form Errors Not Linked to Fields
desc: When a form shows an error message, screen readers do not announce it. The error message has no code-level link to the input field.
fix: Use aria-describedby to connect the error message to its input field. When errors appear, move keyboard focus to the first field with an error so all users know where to fix the problem.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.1: Status Messages (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - ARIA Live Misuse

title: Form Field Has Conflicting Labels
desc: A form field has both a visible label and an aria-label that say different things. Screen reader users hear the aria-label while sighted users read the visible label, which creates confusion.
fix: Use only one labeling method, or make sure both labels say the same thing. The accessible name (aria-label or aria-labelledby) must contain the visible label text.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Info and Relationships (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - Accessible Names

fix: Provide a visible `<label>` with matching `for` and `id` attributes. If not possible, use `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
title: Unlabeled Select or Dropdown
desc: `<select>` or custom dropdown lacks a label. AT users cannot determine the choice they are making.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Info and Relationships (Level A)
WebAIM: Creating Accessible Forms - Form Controls
Deque University - Form elements must have labels

title: Layout Breaks When Text Is Enlarged
desc: When users increase text size in their browser to 200%, the page layout breaks. Text overlaps other content, gets cut off, or disappears. Low vision users who rely on larger text cannot read the page.
fix: Use flexible layouts and relative units (rem, em, %) instead of fixed pixel heights. Test the page at 200% text size in your browser settings to make sure everything remains readable and nothing overflows.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.4: Reflow (Level AA)

title: Vague or Generic Link Text
desc: Links use generic text like "Click here", "Read more", or "Learn more". Screen reader users who navigate by links cannot tell where each link goes.
fix: Write link text that describes the destination or action. Instead of "Click here", use "Download the accessibility checklist" or "Read the full WCAG 1.1.1 explanation".

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - On Link Underlines

title: Media Has No Transcript or Captions
desc: A video or audio recording has no captions or transcript. Deaf and hard of hearing users cannot access the spoken content.
fix: For audio-only content, provide a full text transcript. For video with audio, provide synchronized captions. Place the transcript near the media or link to it clearly. Auto-generated captions must be reviewed and corrected before publishing.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.2.1: Captions (Live) (Level A)
Deque - Multimedia Accessibility: Is it important?

title: List Content Not Using List Markup
desc: Content that looks like a list ,  such as navigation links, steps, or options ,  is built with divs or paragraphs instead of HTML list elements. Screen readers cannot announce how many items are in the list.
fix: Use ul for unordered lists, ol for numbered lists, and dl for definition-style lists. Pair each list with li or dt/dd items. This also helps with navigation menus and step-by-step instructions.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Multi-Pointer Gesture Without Alternative
desc: A feature requires a multi-finger gesture ,  like pinch-to-zoom or a two-finger swipe ,  with no single-tap or keyboard alternative. Users with motor disabilities who cannot perform multi-touch gestures are locked out.
fix: Provide a single-pointer alternative for every multi-point gesture. For example, add plus and minus zoom buttons alongside pinch-to-zoom. All gestures must have a keyboard-accessible equivalent.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.1: Pointer Gestures (Level A)

title: Vague Error Message
desc: A form shows an error when the user submits, but the message does not say how to fix it. For example, it say "Invalid input" without explaining what format is expected.
fix: Write specific, actionable error messages. Tell users exactly what went wrong and how to correct it. For example: "Phone number must be 10 digits, numbers only" instead of "Invalid phone number".

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.3: Error Identification (Level AA)
Adrian Roselli - Form Validation & Errors

title: Video Has No Closed Captions
desc: A prerecorded video has spoken audio but no captions. Deaf and hard of hearing users cannot access the spoken content, and users watching in noisy or sound-sensitive environments cannot follow along.
fix: Add accurate captions to every prerecorded video that has a spoken audio track. Captions must be synchronized with the audio, include speaker identification where relevant, and describe important non-speech sounds (like [applause] or [doorbell]). Review auto-generated captions for accuracy before publishing.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.2.2: Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A)
Deque - Multimedia Accessibility: Is it important?

title: Video Has No Audio Description
desc: A prerecorded video contains visual information that is not described in the audio ,  such as on-screen text, actions, or diagrams. Blind and low vision users miss this content entirely.
fix: Add an audio description track that narrates key visual content during natural pauses in the dialogue. If there are not enough pauses, create an extended audio description version with the video paused at relevant moments. An alternative is a full text description, but an audio track is preferred.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.2.5: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level AA)
Deque - Multimedia Accessibility: Is it important?

fix: Warn users at least 20 seconds before a time limit expires and provide an accessible mechanism to extend or disable it. Use auto-save where possible to preserve partial progress.
title: Session Expires Without Warning
desc: A timed session expires without warning the user or offering a way to extend it. Users of assistive technology who move through content more slowly lose their work without any opportunity to intervene.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.2.1: Timing Adjustable (Level A)

title: Uncontrolled Flashing Content
scLabel: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A)
desc: Content on the page flashes or blinks more than 3 times per second. Rapidly flashing content trigger photosensitive seizures, which are a medical emergency.
fix: Remove or redesign any content that flashes more than 3 times per second. If flashing is needed, reduce the frequency to 3 times per second or below and ensure the flashing area is small. Test animated GIFs, CSS animations, and video clips. Use the Photosensitive Epilepsy Analysis Tool (PEAT) for borderline cases.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.3.1: Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A)
Deque - Supporting Design: Accessibility Heuristics Evaluation

title: Content Does Not Reflow at High Zoom
desc: When zoomed to 400% in the browser, the page requires horizontal scrolling to read content. Low vision users who zoom in lose context when content flows off-screen instead of wrapping.
fix: Design content so it remains readable in a single scrolling direction at the equivalent of a 320 CSS pixel viewport width. Use flexible layouts, relative units (rem, em, %), and avoid fixed pixel widths on containers. Test by setting browser zoom to 400% on a 1280px-wide window, or by setting the viewport to 320px wide in DevTools.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.10: Reflow (Level AA)
Eric Bailey - Responsive Design

title: Touch Target Too Small
desc: Interactive elements ,  such as buttons, links, and icon controls ,  are smaller than 24�24 CSS pixels with insufficient spacing around them. Small targets are difficult to activate accurately for users with motor disabilities and touch screen users.
fix: Make all interactive targets at least 24�24 CSS pixels, including any spacing offset to neighboring targets. If the visible element is smaller, add padding to expand the clickable area without changing the visual design. Aim for 44�44 CSS pixels on touch interfaces.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA)
Deque - Touch Target Size | Axe DevTools for Mobile

title: Screen Orientation Locked
desc: Content is locked to a single screen orientation (portrait or landscape). It will not reflow when the user rotates their device.
fix: Remove any code that forces a fixed screen orientation. Support both portrait and landscape using CSS media queries or flexible layouts. Only restrict orientation when a specific orientation is essential ,  such as a piano keyboard that only makes sense in landscape.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.4: Orientation (Level AA)

title: Expanded or Collapsed State Not Communicated
desc: A button that opens or closes a panel, accordion, menu, or disclosure widget does not communicate whether the content is currently open or closed. Screen reader users cannot tell the current state from the button alone.
fix: Add aria-expanded="false" to the trigger button by default and toggle it to aria-expanded="true" when the content opens. Update the value every time the state changes. Do not rely on visual indicators like a chevron icon ,  those are not perceived by screen reader users.

links.text: Understanding SC 4.1.2: Content on Hover or Focus (Level A)

title: Device Motion Feature Has No Alternative
desc: A feature is triggered by device motion (such as shaking to undo or tilting to scroll) with no alternative way to perform the same action. Users who cannot move their device or whose device is mounted to a wheelchair cannot access this feature.
fix: Provide a UI control (such as a button or menu option) that performs the same action as the device motion gesture. Also allow users to disable the motion trigger to prevent accidental activation.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.4: Labels or Instructions (Level A)

title: Reading Order Disrupted by CSS Positioning
desc: CSS properties like order, position: absolute, or float cause content to appear in a different visual order. The reading order does not match how users see the page.
fix: Ensure the DOM order matches the intended reading order. If CSS repositioning is necessary, test with a screen reader to confirm the content sequence makes sense. Avoid relying on the CSS order property to define meaning ,  use it only for visual adjustments when the DOM order is already correct.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.2: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A)

title: Focus Indicator Below Minimum Area
desc: The keyboard focus indicator is present but does not meet the WCAG 2.2 minimum requirements. The indicator area must be at least as large as the perimeter of the focused component times 2 CSS pixels, and must have sufficient contrast between focused and unfocused states.
fix: Use a focus outline that is at least 2 CSS pixels thick around the full perimeter of the component. Ensure at least a 3:1 contrast ratio between the focused and unfocused appearance. A solid 2px offset outline that encircles the component and changes color on focus is a reliable approach.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.11: Info and Relationships (Level AA)

title: Instructions Rely on Sensory Characteristics Only
keywords: click the button on the right
desc: Instructions for using the interface describe content by its visual appearance, shape, or position only ,  for example: "Click the round button" or "See the options on the right". Users who cannot see the screen cannot follow these instructions.
fix: Always accompany visual references with the element's name or function. Instead of "Click the button on the right", write "Click the Settings button". Instead of "See the items below", reference the heading or label by name. Never rely on shape, color, or position as the only way to identify something.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.3: Labels or Instructions (Level A)

title: Navigation Changes Position Across Pages
desc: Navigation location changes from page to page. Users who rely on consistent placement (including screen reader users) become confused. They expect to find navigation in the same spot on every page.
fix: Keep navigation menus in the same relative order and position on every page. If new items are added to navigation, insert them consistently so the rest of the order is preserved. Users personalize their own navigation, but the default layout must remain the same across pages.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.2.3: Language of Parts (Level AA)

title: Emoji and Special Characters Disrupt Announcement
desc: Emoji or special characters are used in ways that disrupt screen reader output. Screen readers announce the full Unicode description of every emoji ,  for example, "face with tears of joy" ,  so repeated or decorative emoji create verbose, disruptive announcements. Special characters like dashes, arrows, or symbols also be read unexpectedly.
fix: Hide purely decorative emoji from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true". If an emoji carries meaning, replace it with visible text or supplement it with a visually hidden text alternative. Avoid using sequences of emoji or special characters to convey information (such as a row of stars to represent a rating). Test the full reading experience with a screen reader before publishing emoji-heavy content.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

title: Native App Ignores Device Orientation
desc: The native app locks its interface to a single orientation (portrait or landscape). Users who mount their device in a fixed position, such as on a wheelchair, cannot use the app.
fix: Remove any code that forces or restricts screen orientation. Use platform layout tools (Auto Layout on iOS, ConstraintLayout on Android) to support both orientations gracefully. Only restrict orientation when a specific orientation is genuinely essential to the functionality.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.4: Parsing (Level AA)

title: No Dark Mode Support
desc: The app does not support dark mode. Users who rely on dark mode ,  including those with photosensitivity, migraines, or low vision ,  cannot use a comfortable or accessible color scheme.
fix: Implement a dark color scheme that respects the system-level dark mode preference. On web, use the prefers-color-scheme media query. On native platforms, respond to the system appearance setting. Ensure all text, icons, and UI elements maintain sufficient contrast in dark mode.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: Non-text Content (Level A)

title: Voice Control Cannot Operate Controls
desc: Voice control users speak the visible label to activate a control. Common causes of failure: accessible names that do not contain the visible text, controls with hidden labels, or image buttons with missing alt text.
fix: Give all controls an accessible name that contains their visible label text. For buttons with icons only, provide an alt attribute or aria-label that includes the visible label. Test with voice control tools.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.3: Info and Relationships (Level A)

fix: Test the full app with an external keyboard connected to the device. All interactive controls must be reachable by Tab and activatable by Enter or Space. Focus must be visible and follow a logical order throughout.
title: No External Keyboard Support on Mobile
desc: The app does not support navigation or interaction using an external Bluetooth or hardware keyboard. Users with motor disabilities who pair a keyboard with their phone or tablet cannot use the app.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Keyboard (Level A)

title: Switch Access Not Supported
desc: The interface cannot be fully operated using Switch Control (iOS) or Switch Access (Android). Switch users navigate by scanning through items sequentially with one or two switches. If items are inaccessible, grouped incorrectly, or the scan order is wrong, switch users cannot reach or activate them.
fix: Test with Switch Control on iOS and Switch Access on Android using auto-scan mode. Ensure all interactive elements are reachable in the scan order, that scan groups are logical, and that no interactive elements are skipped. Avoid focus traps. Custom components must expose the correct accessibility traits so the platform include them in the scan.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Error Identification (Level A)
Adrian Roselli - Form Feedback

title: Visible Heading Not Marked as Heading
desc: Text looks like a heading (large, bold, or visually distinct). However, it is not marked up as a heading in code. Screen reader users cannot navigate by heading or tell the text is important. Assistive technology cannot accurately describe the page structure.
fix: Replace the styled element with the appropriate heading element (h1 through h6). The heading level should reflect the document outline, not the visual size. Use CSS to control appearance separately from semantic level. Confirm the heading fits logically into the existing heading hierarchy on the page.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: Dragging Movements (Level A)

title: Heading Does Not Describe the Section
desc: A heading does not describe the topic or purpose of the section it introduces. Generic headings like "More information", "Section 1", or "Details" give screen reader users navigating the heading list no useful information about the content that follows.
fix: Write headings that describe the specific content of the section they introduce. Avoid generic labels ,  instead of "Details", use the subject matter such as "Shipping and Returns" or "Eligibility Requirements". Every heading should make sense when read in isolation on the page heading list.

links.text: TPGi: When do headings fail WCAG?

title: Audio or Video Autoplays Without Controls
desc: Audio or video content starts playing automatically and continues for more than 3 seconds without a mechanism to pause, stop, or mute it. This disrupts screen reader users whose speech output competes with the auto-playing audio.
fix: Do not autoplay audio or video that contains sound. If autoplay is required for a legitimate reason, provide a clearly labeled pause, stop, or mute control at the very top of the page ,  before the media in the DOM. On web, avoid the autoplay attribute on <audio> and <video> elements unless the content is muted.

links.text: Deque axe rule: no-autoplay-audio

title: Text Embedded in an Image
desc: Text is rendered inside an image rather than as real HTML text. Users who need to resize text, change fonts, increase letter spacing, or use a high-contrast color scheme cannot do so ,  the text is locked inside the image at a fixed size and style.
fix: Replace text-in-images with real HTML text styled with CSS. If a specific visual treatment is essential (such as a logo), provide equivalent alt text on the image. Avoid images for banners, buttons, callouts, or any content that conveys meaningful information. Canvas elements that render text are also covered by this criterion ,  canvas text cannot be resized, reflowed, or read by assistive technology; use HTML or SVG instead.

links.text: Deque: Use real text, not images of text

title: Placeholder Used as the Only Label
desc: A form input uses placeholder text as its only label. Placeholder text disappears the moment the user starts typing, leaving no reminder of what the field requires. Placeholder text also typically fails minimum contrast requirements and is not reliably announced as a label by all screen readers.
fix: Use a persistent <label> element associated with every input via matching for and id attributes. Placeholder be used as a supplementary example or hint alongside a real label, but never as the sole means of identifying the field. If space is limited, use a visually hidden label that remains in the DOM.

links.text: Smashing Magazine: Don't Use The Placeholder Attribute

title: Single-Char Shortcut Cannot Be Remapped
desc: The page implements keyboard shortcuts using a single character ,  a letter, number, or punctuation mark ,  that cannot be turned off or remapped to a modifier-key combination. Speech input users who dictate text accidentally trigger these shortcuts mid-dictation.
fix: Provide a settings mechanism to turn off or remap single-character shortcuts to combinations that require a modifier key (Ctrl, Alt, Shift). Alternatively, make shortcuts active only when a specific component holds keyboard focus, so they cannot fire during free-form text entry.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.4: Contrast (Minimum) (Level A)
WebAIM - Contrast Checker

title: Authentication Requires Solving a Cognitive Test
desc: The authentication or login flow requires users to memorize, transcribe, or solve a cognitive function test ,  such as copying characters from a distorted image, solving a math problem, or recalling a secret code ,  with no alternative method available.
fix: Provide at least one authentication method that does not require a cognitive test. Acceptable approaches include: allowing paste into password and username fields, supporting password managers and autofill, using email-link or OAuth sign-in, or using an object-recognition CAPTCHA where users click images rather than transcribe text.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.8: Page Titled (Level AA)

title: Positive Tabindex Disrupts Focus Order
desc: Elements use positive tabindex values (tabindex="1", tabindex="2", etc.) to manually control keyboard focus sequence. Positive tabindex creates a separate priority tab ring that is nearly impossible to maintain correctly as content changes, and routinely produces confusing or unpredictable focus order.
fix: Remove all positive tabindex values. Use tabindex="0" to include a custom element in the natural tab order, and tabindex="-1" to make an element focusable by script without placing it in the tab sequence. Correct focus order by reordering elements in the DOM rather than overriding it with tabindex.

links.text: Deque: Don't use positive tabindex values

title: ARIA Menu Roles on Navigation Links
desc: Navigation links use role="menu" and role="menuitem" ARIA roles. These roles signal a widget that should respond to arrow-key navigation (like a desktop application menu), but site navigation links use the Tab key. Screen readers enter a special interaction mode for menus and users expect a different keyboard contract, making the navigation confusing or broken.
fix: Use a <nav> element with a <ul>/<li> list of <a> links for site navigation. Do not apply role="menu" or role="menuitem" to navigation. If you need a true application menu (e.g. a toolbar with File/Edit/View actions), the ARIA menu pattern is appropriate ,  but only when arrow-key navigation between items is fully implemented.

links.text: Adrian Roselli: Don't Use ARIA Menu Roles for Site Nav

title: CSS display Property Removes Semantics
desc: An element uses CSS display:contents, which removes the element's own box from the layout but keeps its children. Many browsers also strip the element's ARIA role, meaning a <button> is no longer announced as a button, a <table> is no longer recognized as a table, and a <ul> is no longer navigable as a list. The rendering looks correct visually but the semantic structure is broken for assistive technology.
fix: Avoid display:contents on elements whose role carries meaning (buttons, links, headings, tables, lists, landmarks). Use a wrapper <div> or <span> for layout purposes instead, and apply display:contents only to that neutral wrapper. Check browser support tables ,  behavior has improved but remains inconsistent.

links.text: Eric Bailey: display:contents considered harmful

title: Interactive Element Nested in Another
desc: A focusable, interactive element (such as a link or button) is nested inside another interactive element. HTML does not permit interactive content descendants inside buttons or links. Screen readers and keyboard-only users encounter unpredictable behavior ,  some AT reads both elements, others only one, and focus order becomes ambiguous.
fix: Separate the nested controls so they are siblings, not parent/child. A common pattern is a "clickable card" where the whole card and an inner link both navigate ,  use a single anchor on the card, or use CSS positioning to extend a single link's click area over the card without nesting. Never place a <button> or <a> inside another <button> or <a>.

links.text: Adrian Roselli: Be wary of nesting roles

title: Custom Scrollbar Overrides User Settings
desc: The page applies custom CSS scrollbar styles that override the operating system's native scrollbars. Custom scrollbars often become invisible or unusable in Windows Forced Colors Mode (High Contrast), ignore OS-level scrollbar width preferences set by low-vision users, and frequently fail the 3:1 non-text contrast requirement.
fix: Remove custom scrollbar CSS (::-webkit-scrollbar, scrollbar-color, scrollbar-width: thin). Let the browser render native scrollbars that automatically adapt to OS accessibility settings including Forced Colors Mode and user-defined scrollbar sizes. If a visible scrollbar track is required for UX reasons, ensure it passes 3:1 contrast in all color schemes including forced-colors.

links.text: Eric Bailey: Don't use custom CSS scrollbars

title: Control Not Keyboard Accessible
desc: The control only be used with a mouse. keyboard-only users cannot focus or activate it. Custom elements built with div or span also lack a role, so screen readers do not know what the control is.
fix: Use native HTML elements like button or a whenever possible ,  they are keyboard accessible by default and have built-in accessible roles. If a custom element is necessary, add tabindex="0", an appropriate ARIA role, and keyboard event handlers for Enter and Space.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Keyboard (Level A)

title: Dynamic Type Scaling Not Supported
desc: The app does not scale with the system font size. On iOS, text is hardcoded to point sizes instead of using Dynamic Type styles (UIFont.preferredFont), so text stays small when users increase it in Settings → Accessibility. On Android, text is set in dp instead of sp, so the Android font scale setting has no effect.
fix: iOS: use UIFont.preferredFont(forTextStyle:) or SwiftUI .font(.body) / .dynamicTypeSize() for all text. Opt the app in with UISupportsDocumentBrowser or set UIApplicationSupportsIndirectInputEvents. Ensure layouts use Auto Layout with flexible constraints so they grow. Android: define all text sizes in sp (scale-independent pixels) in your styles. Test by changing system font size to "Largest" in Settings. Use spannable text if you need mixed sizes.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.4: Info and Relationships (Level AA)

fix: Provide non-gesture alternatives for every gesture-based action: add visible delete/edit buttons, offer long-press menus, implement accessibility actions (iOS `AccessibilityAction`, Android custom actions). Never delete or confirm important actions through gesture alone. Test with Switch Control (iOS) and Voice Access (Android).
title: Custom Gestures Without Non-Gesture Alternatives
desc: App uses custom gestures (swipe-to-delete, pinch-to-zoom, drag-to-reorder) as the only method to trigger actions. Users with motor impairments, switch control users, and voice control users cannot perform complex gestures and are blocked from using core features.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Audio Control (Level A)

fix: On iOS, use `AccessibilityElement` and set `AccessibilitySortPriority` to enforce focus order. On Android, use `importantForAccessibility` and verify nesting structure respects logical order. Test navigation with actual VoiceOver/TalkBack through realistic user workflows (e.g., entering a form, navigating a list). Ensure heading, section, and control order matches visual top-to-bottom, left-to-right flow.
title: Semantic Focus Order Illogical
desc: VoiceOver (iOS) or TalkBack (Android) navigation order jumps around illogically, skips interactive elements, or navigates against visual reading order. Screen reader users cannot predict where focus will move, breaking the ability to navigate the app reliably.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.3: Focus Order (Level A)

fix: Use `enableEdgeToEdgeLayout()` and test all swipe gestures against system back navigation. Avoid swipe-based shortcuts; provide button alternatives. If a gesture is necessary, use `SystemGestureExclusion` carefully and document the behavior. Always ensure a clear non-gesture way to navigate (buttons, menus). Test on Android 10+ devices with gesture navigation enabled.
title: Custom Gestures Conflict with System Navigation
desc: Android 10+ introduces system gesture navigation (swipe from edges to go back). Custom app gestures (swipe-left for menu, swipe-right for action) conflict with system navigation. Users cannot back out of screens or the gesture is unpredictably interpreted as system or app action, trapping users or breaking navigation.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Keyboard (Level A)
WAI-ARIA APG

title: Focus Not Managed
desc: When a modal, dialog, or drawer opens, keyboard focus stays where it was. Screen reader and keyboard-only users cannot easily reach the new content.
fix: Move focus to the first element inside the new content when it opens. Use tabindex="-1" on a heading if the first focusable element comes later. focus trap inside while it is open, and return focus to the trigger button when it closes.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.3: 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)

title: Focus Indicator Missing or Not Visible
desc: keyboard-only users cannot see which element is focused. The default focus outline be removed, or the custom focus style is too faint to see clearly.
fix: Make sure every keyboard-focusable element shows a clear focus outline. Do not set outline: none without providing a visible custom focus style. The focus indicator must have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against nearby colors.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.7: 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)

title: Text Contrast Too Low
desc: Text does not have enough contrast against its background. People with low vision or color blindness not be able to read it.
fix: Change the text color, background color, or both so the contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1. Use a color contrast checker tool to verify.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.3: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA)

title: Skip Link Not Visible When Focused
desc: A skip link exists but is hidden from sighted keyboard-only users. When a keyboard-only user tabs to it, nothing appears on screen.
fix: Make the skip link appear on screen when it receives keyboard focus. It be hidden off-screen by default, but must become visible when focused.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.7: 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)

title: Incorrect Heading Structure
desc: Heading levels are used in a way that does not match the document structure. For example, an h3 appear before an h2 in the same section, or a subheading uses a higher level number than its parent. Screen reader users rely on the heading hierarchy to understand how information is organized. When heading structure is wrong, users cannot navigate the page correctly.
fix: Assign heading levels based on document structure, not visual styling. If a section is conceptually a sub-item, it should use a lower-numbered heading than its parent. Important: skipping heading levels (for example, h1 then h3) is a best practice but not a WCAG failure. Reversing hierarchy (using a higher number for a more prominent section) does fail this criterion.

links.text: TPGi: When do headings fail WCAG?

title: No H1 on the Page
desc: The page has no h1 heading. WCAG does not require an h1, but including one is strongly recommended ,  it names the page topic and is the most predictable entry point when screen reader users navigate by heading.
fix: Add a single h1 to each page that names the main topic or page title. All other section headings should use h2 through h6 in descending order below it. Multiple h1s on a single page should be avoided.

links.text: TPGi: When do headings fail WCAG?

title: Asterisk for Required Fields Not Explained
desc: The form uses asterisks (*) to mark required fields, but the meaning of the asterisk is never explained. Some users not know what it means.
fix: Add a note at the top of the form that explains the asterisk, such as "Fields marked with * are required." Also add the required or aria-required attribute to each required field so screen readers announce it as required.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.2: 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A)

title: ARIA Used Incorrectly
desc: ARIA attributes are applied incorrectly. Common problems: aria-hidden is placed on a focusable element, role="alert" is used for routine messages, or ARIA roles conflict with the element's native behavior.
fix: Follow the ARIA specification closely. Never put aria-hidden on an element that is focusable or contains focusable children. Use role="alert" only for urgent, time-sensitive messages ,  use aria-live="polite" for everything else.

links.text: Understanding SC 4.1.2: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)

title: Zoom or Pinch-to-Zoom Disabled
desc: The page prevents users from zooming in using a browser or pinch gesture. People with low vision rely on zooming to read content.
fix: Remove user-scalable="no" from the viewport meta tag. Do not set maximum-scale below 2. Allow users to zoom freely.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.4.4: 1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA)

title: Text Input Missing a Label
desc: A text input, textarea, or similar field has no visible label. Its label is not linked to the field at the code level.
fix: Give every form field a visible label element that describes what to enter. Link the label to the input using matching for and id attributes. Avoid using placeholder text as the only label.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Hidden Content Readable by Screen Readers
desc: Content that is visually hidden (such as a closed dropdown or collapsed panel) is still readable by screen readers. Users hear content that seems to have no context.
fix: Use display: none or visibility: hidden to hide content from both visual and screen reader users. Or use aria-hidden="true" on content that should be invisible to screen readers. Make sure the chosen method actually hides the content from assistive technology.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Accessible Name Does Not Match Label
desc: A control's accessible name is different from its visible text label. Voice input users speak the visible label to activate the control, but it does not match what the control is actually named.
fix: Ensure the accessible name contains the exact visible label text. Do not add extra words to the accessible name. Voice input users speak the visible text, not extra descriptive labels.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.3: 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A)

title: Incorrect ARIA Tabs Implementation
desc: The component uses ARIA tabs, which require arrow key navigation that many users do not expect. ARIA tab patterns are easy to break and hard to implement correctly.
fix: Consider replacing ARIA tabs with a simpler pattern. Accordion, links, or a button-panel structure often provide the same content without the added complexity.

links.text: Understanding SC N/A: Best Practice

title: Non-interactive Element in Tab Order
desc: A non-interactive element (such as a div, paragraph, or progress bar) is in the tab order. keyboard-only users tab to it but cannot do anything with it, which is confusing.
fix: Remove the tabindex attribute from non-interactive elements. Only native interactive elements or elements that need programmatic focus (such as dialog headings) should receive focus.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.3: 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)

title: Repeated Links to the Same Destination
desc: A content block has multiple separate links or buttons that all point to the same destination. For example, a card have a linked image, a linked title, and a "Read more" button. keyboard-only users must tab through every link, and screen reader users hear the same destination announced multiple times.
fix: Combine them into a single link. Mark the image as decorative (alt="") and use the text as the link label. Or wrap the entire card in one link element.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.4: 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A)

title: Drag Action Has No Keyboard Alternative
desc: A feature requires the user to drag an element with a pointer. There is no keyboard-accessible way to perform the same action.
fix: Provide keyboard-accessible controls (such as buttons) that perform the same action as dragging. keyboard-only users should be able to complete every task without a mouse.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.5.7: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA)

title: Page Landmarks Missing or Incorrect
desc: Page content is not organized inside HTML landmark elements. Screen reader users cannot jump between sections of the page ,  they must read everything from the start.
fix: Wrap all page content in semantic HTML elements: header, nav, main, aside, and footer. Every page needs at least one main element. Use landmark roles only when the right HTML element is not available.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Page Title Does Not Change
desc: The page title (shown in the browser tab) stays the same on all pages. Users cannot tell which page they are on from the tab alone.
fix: Update the document title on each page to describe what that page is about. For example: "Cart ,  My Store" or "Settings ,  App Name". In a single-page app, update the title on each route change.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.2: 2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)

title: Chart Missing Text Alternative
desc: Charts and graphs convey data visually but have no text alternative. Screen reader users cannot access the information the chart contains.
fix: Provide a text summary that describes what the chart shows ,  its type, key trends, and main takeaways. When possible, also provide the underlying data in a table.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A)

title: Tab Order Mismatches Visual Order
desc: When tabbing through the page, focus jumps in an order that does not match what is shown on screen. This is confusing for keyboard-only users.
fix: Make the HTML source order match the visual layout. Avoid using positive tabindex values to control tab order ,  they create maintenance problems and usually make things worse.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.4.3: 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)

title: Informative Content Hidden from Screen Readers
desc: Content that carries meaning (like a star rating or status icon) is hidden from screen readers using aria-hidden. Screen reader users cannot access that information.
fix: Remove aria-hidden from content that carries meaning. Add an accessible name or supplemental text that conveys the same information. For example, instead of hiding a star rating, add hidden text like "Rating: 4 out of 5 stars".

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A)

title: Changing an Input Causes Unexpected Change
desc: Selecting an option in a dropdown or changing a form value automatically causes the page to reload or navigate. Users who keyboard through a list of options trigger an unintended change.
fix: Do not trigger page-level changes when the user changes a form value. Instead, wait for a deliberate submit action ,  like pressing a "Go" button ,  before acting on the selection.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.2.2: 3.2.2 On Input (Level A)

title: Content Announced Incorrectly by Screen Readers
desc: Content is formatted in a way that causes screen readers to read it incorrectly. For example, a price of "$1,200" be read as garbled text depending on how it is marked up. On native apps, incorrect accessibility labels or groupings cause VoiceOver or TalkBack to announce content that is out of order or missing context.
fix: Test the content with the target screen reader ,  VoiceOver, TalkBack, or NVDA/JAWS. On web, fix the HTML markup or text formatting. On native, review accessibility labels, container groupings, and element ordering so the announced output conveys the intended meaning accurately.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Figure or Illustration Has No Description
desc: An image or diagram uses a figure element but has no figcaption or accessible description. Screen reader users hear the image file name or a generic announcement instead of what the image shows.
fix: Add a figcaption element inside the figure that explains what the image shows or why it matters. For more complex visuals, link to a longer text description nearby.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A)

title: Dropdown or Select Has No Label
desc: A select element or custom dropdown has no label. Screen reader users hear the control announced without context, for example hearing the options without knowing whether the field is for country, language, or quantity.
fix: Add a visible label element with a for attribute that matches the select element's id. If you cannot show a visible label, use aria-label or aria-labelledby instead.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Form Group Has No Group Label
desc: A group of related form controls (like radio buttons or checkboxes) has no group label. Screen reader users hear each option without understanding what question it answers.
fix: Wrap the group in a fieldset element and add a legend as its first child. The legend text should be the question or category the group belongs to. For example: "Choose your preferred contact method".

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.1: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)

title: Dynamic Updates Not Announced
desc: Content that updates dynamically ,  like a search result count, a progress update, or a notification ,  is not announced by screen readers. On web, the live region is missing or misconfigured. On native iOS, UIAccessibilityPostNotification is not called; on Android, View.announceForAccessibility or AccessibilityEvent.TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED is missing.
fix: Web: mark status regions with role="status" (polite) or role="alert" (assertive), or aria-live="polite/assertive". Keep the region in the DOM at page load; only update its content, do not inject it later. Native iOS: call UIAccessibilityPostNotification(UIAccessibilityLayoutChangedNotification, messageElement) or UIAccessibilityAnnouncementNotification for one-off messages. Native Android: use View.announceForAccessibility("Message") or AccessibilityManager.sendAccessibilityEvent with TYPE_ANNOUNCEMENT.

links.text: Understanding SC 4.1.3: 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA)

title: Autocomplete Attribute Missing on Personal Data Fields
desc: Form fields that collect personal information ,  such as name, email, phone number, and address ,  are missing the autocomplete attribute. Users with motor disabilities or cognitive impairments who rely on browser autofill must enter data manually every time.
fix: Add the autocomplete attribute to all personal data fields using the correct HTML token values. For example: autocomplete="name", autocomplete="email", autocomplete="tel", autocomplete="street-address", autocomplete="new-password". A full list of valid values is available in the HTML specification.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.3.5: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (Level AA)

title: Iframe Missing a Title
desc: An iframe element does not have a title attribute. Screen reader users cannot tell what the embedded content is before they enter it ,  they hear only "frame" with no context.
fix: Add a descriptive title attribute to every iframe. For example: <iframe title="Google Maps showing our office location">. If the iframe contains no meaningful content, hide it from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true".

links.text: Understanding SC 4.1.2: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)

title: No Confirmation Step for Irreversible Actions
desc: An action cannot be easily undone (such as deleting data, completing a purchase, or submitting). There is no confirmation step to prevent accidental activation.
fix: Before completing any significant or irreversible action, give users a chance to review, confirm, or cancel. Options include a confirmation dialog, a review-and-edit summary screen, or a brief undo window after the action completes. Clearly label destructive actions so users understand the consequence before they commit.

links.text: Understanding SC 3.3.4: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA)

title: No External Keyboard Support
desc: The mobile app does not support navigation or interaction using an external Bluetooth or hardware keyboard. Users with motor disabilities who pair a keyboard with their phone or tablet cannot use the app.
fix: Test the full app with an external keyboard connected to the device. All interactive controls must be reachable by Tab key and activatable by Enter or Space. Focus must be visible at all times, and focus order must follow a logical sequence. On iOS, implement UIKeyCommand and ensure all focusable elements are keyboard-reachable. On Android, handle key events appropriately.

links.text: Understanding SC 2.1.1: 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)

title: Linked Document Is Not Accessible
desc: A link points to a PDF or Word document that is not accessible. Common problems include scanned PDFs without a text layer, untagged PDFs, or PDFs with missing alt text. Users cannot read the document or navigate its content.
fix: Convert the document to accessible PDF format. Add text layer to scanned PDFs, tag elements, and add alt text. Or provide an accessible HTML version as the primary link.

links.text: Understanding SC 1.1.1: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A)

title: Custom Accessibility Actions Not Provided
desc: Contextual actions that are available through swipe gestures, long-press menus, or custom interactions are not exposed to assistive technology. VoiceOver users cannot swipe up/down to reveal actions, and TalkBack users have no equivalent accessibility action. Users who cannot perform complex gestures are locked out of these features.
fix: iOS: add UIAccessibilityCustomAction objects to the accessibilityCustomActions array of the view. Provide a clear name and a handler block. For list rows with swipe actions, implement accessibilityCustomActions to mirror each swipe option (Delete, Reply, Archive, etc.). Android: override onInitializeAccessibilityNodeInfo and call info.addAction() with a custom AccessibilityNodeInfoCompat.AccessibilityActionCompat. For RecyclerView items, expose each contextual action this way. Test with VoiceOver (swipe up/down on the element) and TalkBack (double-tap-hold then drag).

links.text: Understanding SC 4.1.2: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)
